effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive percentages from the N = 150 household survey and secondary municipal figures are reported alongside qualitative DPSIR synthesis; no inferential statistical tests, regression coefficients, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Municipal agencies supply piped water to only 27% of Guwahati's population, leaving 69% directly dependent on groundwater (~79 MLD extraction, exceeding safe yield). Under weak governance—groundwater rights tied to land ownership (Indian Easements Act, 1882), an unimplemented Assam Groundwater Control and Regulation Act, 2012, and non-enforcement of green-belt/eco-sensitive land-use rules—100% of surveyed households (150/150 across 3 unserved wards) constructed wells without permits, fees, spacing norms, or monitoring. Over the prior 5 years, 78% of surveyed households in central Ward 35 and 82% in southern Ward 57 reported groundwater level decline (vs. 84% reporting unchanged levels in western Ward 02), prompting shifts to deeper drilled wells (56% in Ward 35; 92% in Ward 57). In depleted Ward 35 (n = 50), 84% of households relied on private water vendors charging ~$4 per 1,000 L, while 12% could not afford vendors and fetched water from distant municipal wells (>1 km) or informal middlemen, spending >5% of income or hours daily ('water-poor').

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the mixed-methods/observational case-study design ceiling. Assigned 2 because the study directly documents the statutory and administrative regulatory vacuum (land-tied groundwater rights under the 1882 Act, unframed rules/unconstituted authorities/unnotified critical areas blocking the 2012 Assam Groundwater Act, and Master Plan non-enforcement) and directly observes its operation at household level (100% of 150 surveyed households reporting unpermitted, fee-free, unmonitored well construction and subsequent aquifer depletion/affordability burdens in unserved wards). Proposed water-use fees and energy tariffs in Section 8.2 are policy recommendations not empirically tested in Guwahati.

evidence_quotes.quote: Overall methodology used the DPSIR framework for which inputs were generated from questionnaire survey of 150 households and other ofﬁcial, literature records.
The groundwater right still comes under the Land right according to the Indian Easements Act,1882, with no regulation or restriction over the quantity of groundwater that should be drawn

The revised ‘Assam Groundwater Control and Regulation Act, 2012’, which comes clear with its purpose and designated ofﬁcers is yet not implemented because the rules that are required for its implementation are yet to be framed, zonal authorities are yet to be constituted and also for the act to be implemented it requires the area to be notiﬁed as ‘critical area’ which is not done yet.

Of the 150 households interviewed, 100% of the respondents stated that there is no regulation and that they constructed wells on their own will without seeking permission from any authority, without paying any form of fee to any of the regulatory bodies
84% of the households in the ward no. 35 answered to have been dependent on private vendors for daily water usage.
